hops.afterHeading: Association, prediction and causation in human imaging
hops.title: Can a brain scan catch a liar in court?
hops.text: Crime dramas treat brain scanners as truth machines. When psychologist Lorne Semrau faced federal healthcare fraud charges, he offered fMRI testimony that he seemed generally truthful when saying his billing was in good faith. The examiner, Steven Laken, had tested his method in mock scenarios with volunteers aged 18 to 50; Semrau was 63. A second scan on another billing topic flagged him as deceptive; citing fatigue, Laken retested that topic nearly two weeks later with shorter questions, obtaining a nondeceptive result. The appeals court called that retest a best two out of three. In 2012 it upheld excluding the testimony, citing no known error rates outside the lab.

sources.citation: United States v. Semrau, 693 F.3d 510 (6th Cir. 2012).

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A wooden gavel on a courtroom bench next to three brain-scan films, two stacked together and one set apart.
image.caption: A scan pattern from lab volunteers does not tell a court whether one particular person is lying.

hops.afterHeading: From manipulation to a scoped causal claim
hops.title: The bull that stopped charging
hops.text: Facing a charging fighting bull, the brain-stimulation pioneer José Delgado pressed a button on a radio transmitter. The signal triggered equipment on the bull to stimulate its brain through implanted electrodes, and the bull stopped its charge. Press accounts cast this as taming aggression; Delgado proposed both a motor effect and inhibited aggressive drive. Elliot Valenstein was less convinced. In his 1973 book Brain Control, he argued that stimulation forced the bull to keep turning in one direction, which could explain why the charge stopped. A bull that stops running has shown you a motor effect; whether its anger changed is a separate question that needs its own measurement.

sources.citation: Schleim S. Neurorights in History: A Contemporary Review of José M. R. Delgado's 'Physical Control of the Mind' (1969) and Elliot S. Valenstein's 'Brain Control' (1973). Front Hum Neurosci. 2021;15:703308.
Marzullo, translation of Delgado's bull-stimulation account. JUNE. 2017;15:R29.
Delgado JMR. Physical Control of the Mind (1969), Chapter 16.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A black bull skidding to a sideways halt in a dusty bullring, with a vintage handheld radio transmitter resting on the railing in the foreground.
image.caption: Stopping a bull's charge showed a motor effect; it did not show that the bull's aggression had gone.

hops.afterHeading: Isolate the cause: light controls and pathway specificity
hops.title: Mice that saw the red laser
hops.text: At equal light reaching the retina, mouse opsins respond less to red than blue. Yet when an Allen Institute team delivered light through a brain fibre during a visual task with no engineered opsin responding, 640-nanometre red light at the highest powers made mice stop more often for unrewarded objects. The authors inferred mice used the red illumination as a cue to stop for low-contrast targets. Blue and yellow light caused no statistically detectable rise in false alarms at tested powers. Red scatters less in brain tissue; stronger responses in the nearer eye made an internal route more likely. A white LED facing that eye almost eliminated the artifact.

sources.citation: Danskin B, Denman D, Valley M, et al. Optogenetics in Mice Performing a Visual Discrimination Task: Measurement and Suppression of Retinal Activation and the Resulting Behavioral Artifact. PLoS ONE. 2015;10(12):e0144760.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A brown lab mouse on a running disk with a lit grey monitor showing a striped target to its right and a small white lamp facing its left eye.
image.caption: Red light delivered into the brain can still reach the retina and change what a mouse does.

audio.title: Three surprises that keep circuit experiments honest
audio.transcript:
Designing a brain experiment sounds straightforward until the brain, and the laboratory around it, starts answering a different question from the one you asked. Here are three true stories about timing, controls and statistics.

First, a puzzle about songbirds and rats. In twenty fifteen, Timothy Otchy, Bence Ölveczky and their colleagues at Harvard silenced a brain region called nucleus interface in songbirds, and motor cortex in rats. Temporarily silenced, these regions seemed essential: the birds' learned songs and the rats' learned movement patterns fell apart. It is tempting to conclude that both regions are needed for these skills. Then the team made permanent lesions in the same places, and both skills recovered on their own. Downstream recordings in the songbird brain offered a plausible explanation. After a permanent lesion of nucleus interface, recordings in a downstream song-control area called H V C showed disrupted activity that recovered within days, alongside the song. That recovery is consistent with the circuit rebalancing itself, though other mechanisms remain possible. An abrupt manipulation can disrupt a downstream neighbour even when the silenced region is not permanently required. So a causal claim belongs to the timing and conditions you actually tested.

Second, a story about who is in the room. In twenty fourteen, Robert Sorge, Jeffrey Mogil and colleagues reported that mice and rats showed less pain behaviour around male experimenters than around female ones. In mice, the cause was a stress response, and a man did not even have to be in the room. Cotton T-shirts that men had worn the night before, set about half a metre from the mice, did the same, as did bedding from unfamiliar intact male mammals and compounds from the human armpit. Now imagine running a pain test with a man present for one group and a woman present for the other. The groups could differ before you ever turn on a laser. Matching who is present, randomizing which animals get each treatment, and scoring blind are not fussy paperwork. They keep you from mistaking a worn T-shirt for a neural circuit.

Finally, human brain imaging. Early on a Saturday morning in spring two thousand five, Craig Bennett bought a whole Atlantic salmon from his local supermarket, about eighteen inches long and three point eight pounds, and put it in an f M R I scanner. The fish was, of course, dead. The team showed it fifteen photographs of people in social situations and asked it to judge what emotion each person was feeling. Later they ran a standard test at each of eight thousand sixty-four tiny locations in the scan, without correcting for running thousands of tests at once. Sixteen locations came out significant, including a neat cluster inside the dead fish's brain cavity. When Bennett and his colleagues Abigail Baird, Michael Miller and George Wolford presented the analysis in two thousand nine, they also applied standard corrections for multiple comparisons, and every one of those locations disappeared. The study won the twenty twelve Ig Nobel Prize in Neuroscience, and it left the field a durable reminder: search enough noisy signals without correction, and even a dead fish appears to be reading human faces.

Check the timing, match the controls, and correct for how many questions you asked. Those checks will not prove a circuit claim on their own, but they help you see which claims your experiment can support.
